Instead, the impact coincided closely with a major mass extinction that devastated marine life.

From fractures near its south pole, material from this ocean is ejected into space as a plume of water vapor and ice particles. These particles offer scientists a rare opportunity to investigate an extraterrestrial ocean without drilling through kilometers of ice.

Science.title: Your gut bacteria may reveal how fast your brain is aging

Science.title: Nanoneedle arrays map RNA in fresh tissue without sequencing or amplification

This spatial context has deepened our understanding of cancer, neurobiology and immunology. Yet as the field advances, an important question remains: How many of these powerful technologies are ready for routine clinical use?

Science.title: Heat-trapping gas once frozen in Arctic ground is slowly leaking and warming the planet
Science.summary: As Ted Schuur stepped along the edges of Smith Lake, a bubble surfaced from the muck underfoot. And then another. They're bubbles of methane, a potent heat-trapping gas made from decomposing plants and animals that had once been stuck in Alaska's frigid permafrost. But that frozen ground is thawing because the Arctic is warming four times faster than the rest of the globe. For thousands of years that frozen ground stored dead plants and animals, but the accelerating thaw is allowing them to decay into methane and carbon dioxide.

Science.title: Gamma-ray search sets new limits on dark matter annihilation in the inner Milky Way
Science.summary: Dark matter could be a type of matter in the universe that does not emit, absorb or reflect detectable light and appears to interact very weakly with regular matter. Although physicists have observed gravitational effects attributed to dark matter, they have not yet been able to determine what it is made of.

Science.title: Nature-strip gardens are a paradise for pollinators in your street
Science.summary: In front of most Australian houses, between the sidewalk and the road, runs a strip of land most people never really think about. In Australia, it's called the nature strip, but it goes by other names in other regions, including a verge, parkway or tree lawn.

Science.title: Taste shapes support for climate-friendly school meals
Science.summary: Students in a new study were neither clearly positive nor negative about more climate-friendly school meals. Whether the food tasted good, was filling and felt familiar played an important role. Students were somewhat more positive about reducing the amount of meat in recipes than about having more all-vegetarian days.

Science.title: Giant fluctuations of focused light reveal hidden correlations in opaque materials
Science.summary: When light travels through a strongly scattering material, such as biological tissue or other disordered opaque media, it follows many different paths and produces a seemingly random speckle pattern. Wavefront shaping makes it possible to control this complex interference and focus light through such materials.

Science.title: How can the same El Niño cause drought in one part of the world and floods in another?
Science.summary: The Pacific Ocean is warming unusually quickly, and this year's El Niño has already surpassed previous records. Forecasters expect it to strengthen even further before approaching its usual peak around December.

Science.title: New reactor design improves plastic feedstock synthesis using oxygen and electricity
Science.summary: A "hidden variable" that can determine the success or failure of a chemical reaction has been found in the immediate vicinity of electrodes.

Science.title: Inka scattered sacred coca leaves over sacrificed llamas, excavation suggests
Science.summary: Deep in Peru's Acarí Valley lie the ruins of Tambo Viejo, an Inka provincial center where excavations have uncovered tasseled sacrificial llamas and brightly adorned guinea pigs. But save for a few seeds and some stored leaves, evidence of how the Inka used one of their most sacred plants in rituals remained elusive. Now, archaeologists have discovered coca leaves still stuck in the wool of some sacrificed llamas.

Science.title: One giant clam contains a month‑by‑month diary of the Great Barrier Reef's climate 200 years ago
Science.summary: When you swim through the azure waters of the Great Barrier Reef, there is one creature on the seafloor that's almost impossible to miss: the giant clam. Its huge, fluted shell frames a soft mantle shimmering with electric blue, green and gold.

Science.title: Diet drinks work as well as water for weight loss, major trial finds
Science.summary: A two-year randomized clinical trial involving 493 adults with overweight or obesity found that diet soft drinks were essentially as effective as water for long-term weight loss and weight maintenance. Participants drinking beverages sweetened with aspartame, acesulfame-K, or sucralose lost a similar amount of weight to those drinking water, while both groups also saw improvements in waist size, body composition, and several metabolic measures.

Science.title: A climate threat may lurk beneath Antarctica's last great unknown
Science.summary: A region of Antarctica with some of the greatest potential to reshape the natural world and human society is also the least scientifically understood and explored.

Science.title: Cry for help as French-Swiss lake dries up
Science.summary: The picturesque Lac des Brenets between France and Switzerland has dried up after a record-breaking hot summer, leaving locals crying out for help to save the lake.

Science.title: Scientists just found a new way to make hydrogen from water
Science.summary: A new light-activated material can efficiently produce hydrogen from water without requiring an additional expensive metal catalyst. Researchers say its unusual sulfur-based chemistry could point toward cheaper and more practical ways to turn sunlight into clean fuel.

Science.title: Do animals experience schadenfreude?
Science.summary: Schadenfreude, ‪or pleasure at seeing another's pain, is a complex emotion. So can animals besides humans experience it?

Science.title: Vitamin D drug may help crack pancreatic cancer’s protective shield
Science.summary: A vitamin D analog may help break down pancreatic cancer’s protective defenses, potentially making tumors more vulnerable to chemotherapy and immune attack. A small clinical trial found encouraging responses, especially in patients whose tumors had high levels of the vitamin D receptor.

Science.title: Too many males to choose from can overwhelm female frogs—and change who gets to mate
Science.summary: If you've ever felt overwhelmed by menu options at a restaurant, cereal varieties at the grocery store or potential partners while scrolling through dating apps, you've experienced choice overload.

Science.title: Scientists find a surprising clue to why the universe’s expansion doesn’t add up
Science.summary: Tiny magnetic fields created shortly after the Big Bang may help explain the long-running disagreement over how fast the universe is expanding. Detailed simulations show that these primordial fields could have changed the formation of hydrogen in the early universe, affecting the cosmic microwave background and the expansion rate inferred from it.

Science.title: New research shows steep and continuing decline in prison population in the US
Science.summary: The U.S. prison population is declining at an accelerating rate, and prison admission rates are predicted to fall an additional 50% within the next two decades, according to new research from University at Albany professor Shawn Bushway.

Science.title: Hungary's dwindling paprika producers battle to save signature spice
Science.summary: Working from before dawn until midnight, farmers Nikoletta Pajsan Nagy and Laszlo Pajsan fought Europe's driest summer ever to save their red pepper harvest in Hungary.

Science.title: Cities keep shelling out taxpayer money for sports stadiums, yet the economics almost never makes sense
Science.summary: Americans are crazy about sports. But whether that passion requires taxpayers to subsidize new facilities every time leagues and franchises ask for them needs rigorous scrutiny.

Science.title: Today's emissions choices could limit Antarctic ice loss and sea-level rise for coastal communities
Science.summary: Cutting greenhouse gas emissions now may limit how much ice Antarctica loses this century and reduce the sea-level rise facing coastal communities, according to findings from a new study.

Science.title: Feeling secure in a group may help dissenters make stronger arguments
Science.summary: When everyone in a meeting voices the same opinion, an organization can miss important warning signs and new ideas. A research team from KAIST suggests that when members feel securely accepted within their group, they can express dissenting opinions in greater detail and more persuasively, and other members may be more willing to use those opinions in decision-making.
